items.title: Harry Styles Performs New Song Written for Liam Payne on Anniversary of His Death
items.summary:
Harry Styles played an unreleased song written for Liam Payne at Madison Square Garden on Friday night, two years to the day after his former One Direction bandmate died. The track, titled "What Is Enough," got its live debut in front of a sold-out room, and Styles introduced it with a short address about loss and friendship.

"I feel incredibly lucky to get to play these shows here in New York, and this building means a lot to me," Styles told the crowd, according to Rolling Stone. "There are so many people in my life, friends and people that I've worked with that I wouldn't have been able to do this without. And two years ago today, I lost one of those friends." He added, "I'm sure a lot of you have been through similar things. I hope you haven't. But really, it's just about looking after each other."

Payne died on Oct. 16, 2024, of injuries sustained in a fall from his hotel room balcony. He was 31. In the two years since, each surviving member of One Direction — Styles, Niall Horan, Louis Tomlinson and Zayn Malik — has released new music in some form.

Styles said he wrote the song roughly two years ago, asking the audience's permission before playing it. The performance came midway through his 30-night Madison Square Garden residency, part of the Together, Together global run of 50 shows across seven cities, supporting his fourth album, Kiss All the Time. Disco, Occasionally, released March 6.

In a March interview with Apple Music's Zane Lowe, Styles described the difficulty of mourning Payne in public. "I think there was a period when he passed away where I really struggled with acknowledging how strange it is to have people kind of own part of your grief in a way," he said, adding that "the greatest way you can honor your friends who pass away is by living your life to the fullest."

"What Is Enough" remains unreleased. Styles' New York residency continues as part of the larger Together, Together itinerary.

items.title: ‘Street Fighter’ Socks $31M, ‘You Can See Everything’ Has Lines Around The Block With $12M+ Docu Milestone – Saturday Update
items.summary:
Street Fighter opened to $31 million domestically this weekend, leading the October box office for Paramount, Legendary and Capcom. The adaptation drew heavily from older men, with moviegoers over 35 accounting for 45 percent of the audience, and premium large formats and Imax screens generating 58 percent of its weekend gross.

The bigger story belongs to A24. The distributor's three-hour Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything, directed by Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder, took in $12 million to $14 million on 855 screens — the second-best documentary opening ever, behind only Fahrenheit 9/11's $23.9 million in 2004. Deadline reported roughly 1,300 sellouts and lines stretching around the block at theaters including the Village East in New York and the Belcourt in Nashville.

The documentary's exit numbers are extraordinary for the form. Screen Engine/Rentrak's PostTrak put its definite recommend at 91 percent and overall positive score at 98 percent, with viewers aged 18 to 34 making up 62 percent of the audience. Forty-one percent bought tickets the day of the screening, and 44 percent attended with a partner. Its top-grossing venues were the AMC Empire, the AMC Kabuki in San Francisco and the AMC Lincoln Square.

A24 premiered the film in secret at Telluride and has run a deliberately thin marketing campaign — an Instagram account with 13,000 followers and two YouTube videos that have drawn 42 million views. RelishMix measured overall awareness at 102 million, roughly 40 percent above comparable independent dramas, aided by Fielder's own Instagram following of one million.

The weekend's casualty was 20th Century Studios' Whalefall, which cost $60 million and opened to $7.5 million. Adapted from Daniel Kraus's thriller novel and shot in California, the film landed a B CinemaScore and a 61 percent definite recommend, with 69 percent of its audience over 25 — the same older demographic Street Fighter absorbed.

Street Fighter's $31 million start runs 19 percent behind Mortal Kombat 2's $38.5 million opening in May, and its B- CinemaScore trails both prior Mortal Kombat films. Families have been slow to turn out, with parents and children under 12 making up 11 percent of attendance so far.

items.title: Iron Maiden Announce Surprise 2027 North American Tour
items.summary:
Iron Maiden have added a 2027 North American tour, billed as the third and final leg of the band's 50th anniversary run. The announcement reverses an earlier plan to step away from live performance next year after the 2026 dates on the Run for Your Lives Tour.

The new itinerary covers 16 shows, opening April 14 in Tacoma, Washington and closing May 11 in Belmont Park, New York. The band will follow that with two festival appearances: Sonic Temple in Columbus, Ohio, and Boardwalk Rock in Ocean City, Maryland.

Bassist Steve Harris explained the change of plans in a statement reported by Rolling Stone. "We've been enjoying this last leg in the USA and Canada so much that we all had a chat and decided we should take the show to parts we missed, particularly the North West and South East," he said. "It just seems fair to our many fans there who have given us tremendous support for so many years."

Harris also framed the festival bookings as a deliberate test. "We have always enjoyed playing the many great festivals that are in Europe and wanted to experience a couple more in the USA," he said. "At festivals you are not just playing to your own fans so it's always a challenge and we all love a challenge!"

Bullet for My Valentine and the Raven Age will open the shows, giving the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame inductees an all-British three-band bill for the first time since 1983. The 2026 leg of Run for Your Lives runs first, with the 2027 dates closing out the anniversary cycle.
